name: Argument against the void
plain_explanation: Anaxagoras argued there is no truly empty space; apparently empty containers, like an inflated skin or a water-clock, actually contain air.
precise_definition: Like Empedocles, Anaxagoras denied the existence of a void, appealing to the observation that devices such as the clepsydra (water-clock) or an inflated skin demonstrate the presence of air where nothing visible seems to be present.
why_it_mattered: This is part of the broader fifth-century debate (continued in the next chapter on the Atomists) over whether motion requires empty space, and it shows the era's characteristic mixture of empirical observation and metaphysical argument.
competing_positions: The Atomists' insistence, discussed in the following chapter, that a void must exist for motion to be possible
